Each firm’s marginal abatement cost rises the more it cleans up. Firm A’s line (\(MAC_A = 2e_A\)) is flatter, cleaning is cheap for A, while Firm B’s (\(MAC_B = 8e_B\)) is steep. A permit market sets a single price, and every firm keeps abating until its own \(MAC\) reaches that price, which is the height where the two curves line up. Because A is the cheaper cleaner, A ends up doing most of the abating and B does little.

Let the cheap firm clean up. Equalizing marginal abatement cost across firms hits the pollution target at least total cost. Forcing every firm to abate the same amount wastes the low-cost firm’s advantage, here trading lets Firm A do most of the work and cuts total cost by 36%.

A factory’s marginal benefit from polluting falls as it pollutes more (\(MB = 100 - 2S\)); the marginal damage to a neighbor rises (\(MD = 2S\)). The efficient level is where they cross, \(S^{*}=25\). Coase’s insight: if property rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, the two parties reach \(S^{*}\) regardless of who holds the right, only the split of the gains changes. In Fig 11.5 below, predict where bargaining ends from each starting right; after the reveal, pick who owns the right and move the pollution level one deal at a time to see the bargaining range close on \(S^{*}\).

The efficient level is where they cross, \(S^{*}=25\). Coase’s insight: if property rights are clear and bargaining is cheap, the two parties reach \(S^{*}\) regardless of who holds the right, and only the split of the gains changes. In Fig 11.5 below, predict where bargaining ends from each starting right; after the reveal, pick who owns the right and move the pollution level one deal at a time to see the bargaining range close on \(S^{*}\).

The downward line is the factory’s marginal benefit from polluting (\(MB = 100 - 2S\)), it falls because the easy, high-value pollution comes first. The upward line is the neighbor’s marginal damage (\(MD = 2S\)), which rises as pollution mounts. They cross at the efficient level \(S^{*} = 25\), where one more unit’s benefit to the factory just equals its harm to the neighbor. The two starting markers show the extremes: the polluter’s right (pollution starts high) and the neighbor’s right (pollution starts at zero).

The upward line is the neighbor’s marginal damage (\(MD = 2S\)), which rises as pollution mounts. They cross at the efficient level \(S^{*} = 25\), where one more unit’s benefit to the factory just equals its harm to the neighbor. Coase’s insight is that if the right is clearly assigned and bargaining is cheap, the two parties trade their way to \(S^{*}\) no matter who holds it, because whenever \(MB \neq MD\) there is a deal that makes both better off. Only the direction of payment changes: with the polluter’s right the neighbor pays it to cut back; with the neighbor’s right the polluter pays for permission to emit some. Efficiency is identical, only the distribution of the gains differs. The theorem breaks down when many parties are involved or bargaining is costly, which is exactly when we fall back on taxes and regulation.

Only the direction of payment changes: with the polluter’s right the neighbor pays it to cut back; with the neighbor’s right the polluter pays for permission to emit some. Rights decide who pays, not the outcome. Start from the polluter’s right (high pollution) and the neighbor pays it to cut back; start from the neighbor’s right (zero pollution) and the polluter pays to be allowed some, either way they meet at \(S^{*}=25\). Efficiency does not depend on the allocation of rights, only on the ability to bargain, which is exactly why Coase fails when transaction costs are high or parties are many.
